glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The LORD appoints Aaron and his sons as priests and gives them holy garments “for glory and for beauty,” so that Aaron carries the names of Israel’s tribes on his shoulders and over his heart before the LORD and bears the plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 28 continues the instructions given on Sinai (chapters 25–31). After the tabernacle and its court, God turns to the priests who will serve there.

glance.html:

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “‘So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the breastplate of judgment over his heart, when he goes into the holy place, as a memorial before the LORD continually.” (Exodus 28:29)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
God now appoints the people who will serve in His dwelling. Aaron and his sons are set apart as priests, and they are given holy garments “for glory and for beauty” (28:2), made by artisans whom God has filled with wisdom. Each garment has a purpose, and the most moving purposes are personal.

On the shoulders of the ephod sit two onyx stones engraved with the names of Israel’s sons: “So Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders as a memorial” (28:12). Over his heart hangs the breastplate with twelve precious stones, each bearing a tribe’s name, so that Aaron carries them “over his heart” whenever he goes before the LORD (28:29). The people are carried on his strength and held close in his love. The breastplate also holds the Urim and Thummim, by which Aaron bears Israel’s need for God’s judgment. His blue robe rings with golden bells as he goes in and out, and on his forehead a gold plate declares HOLINESS TO THE LORD, so that the people’s offerings may be accepted before God.

All of this looks ahead to Jesus, our great High Priest, who bears His people before the Father and always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 4:14–16; 7:25).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 28:1–5 — Aaron and His Sons Are Set Apart, and Holy Garments Are Commanded

The LORD tells Moses to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests and to make holy garments for Aaron for glory and beauty. Skilled artisans whom God has filled with wisdom are to make the breastplate, ephod, robe, tunic, turban, and sash.

Exodus 28:6–14 — The Ephod and the Names on Aaron’s Shoulders

The ephod is woven of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with two onyx stones on its shoulder straps, each engraved with six names of Israel’s sons. Aaron carries their names on his shoulders before the LORD as a memorial.

Exodus 28:15–30 — The Breastplate of Judgment over Aaron’s Heart

The breastplate holds twelve precious stones in four rows, each engraved with a tribe’s name, and is fastened to the ephod with gold chains, rings, and a blue cord. Aaron carries Israel’s names over his heart in the holy place, along with the Urim and Thummim for bearing Israel’s judgment before the LORD.

Exodus 28:31–35 — The Blue Robe with Bells and Pomegranates

The robe of the ephod is all blue, with a strong opening for the head and a hem of pomegranates and golden bells. The bells sound whenever Aaron goes into the holy place and comes out, so that he will not die.

Exodus 28:36–38 — The Gold Plate Engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD

A plate of pure gold engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD is fastened to the front of Aaron’s turban. Aaron bears the guilt connected with Israel’s holy gifts so that the people may be accepted before the LORD.

Exodus 28:39–43 — Garments for the Priests’ Ministry

Aaron receives his tunic, turban, and sash, and his sons receive tunics, sashes, and caps for glory and beauty, to be anointed and set apart as priests. Linen undergarments are made so that they will not incur guilt and die when they serve.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 28 shows that God provides someone to stand before Him on His people’s behalf. Aaron bore the names of Israel’s sons on his shoulders and over his heart when he went into the holy place, as a memorial before the LORD (28:12, 29). Jesus is the High Priest of whom Aaron was only a shadow. He carries His people in His strength and holds them on His heart, and He always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25).

The chapter also gives a pattern for how believers serve one another in Christ. Assured that Jesus bears us, we can bear others before the Father in prayer, help carry their burdens, and keep them close to our hearts (Galatians 6:2). Both the shoulders and the heart matter, strength that carries and love that keeps.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
A priesthood appointed by God. God chooses Aaron and his sons to minister to Him (28:1, 41).

Glory and beauty. The holy garments honor the priestly calling (28:2, 40).

Names on shoulders and heart. Aaron carries Israel before the LORD in strength and love (28:12, 29).

Bearing Israel’s judgment. The Urim and Thummim and the gold plate show Aaron representing the people before God (28:30, 38).

Holiness to the LORD. The priest is set apart to God, and approaching Him requires obedience (28:35–38, 43).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Ephod (28:6). The high priest’s richly woven outer garment, with shoulder straps holding two onyx stones.

Breastplate of judgment (28:15). A square pouch worn over the high priest’s chest, set with twelve stones bearing the tribes’ names.

Urim and Thummim (28:30). Sacred lots kept in the breastplate for seeking God’s judgment (Numbers 27:21). Scripture does not describe their shape or exactly how they were used.

HOLINESS TO THE LORD (28:36). The words engraved on the gold plate on Aaron’s turban, declaring that he belonged to God.

Memorial (28:12, 29). Something that keeps a person or event before God. Aaron carries Israel’s names as a memorial before the LORD.

focus: Exodus 28 appoints Aaron and his sons to serve the LORD as priests and describes the holy garments made “for glory and for beauty” (Exodus 28:2). The chapter moves from the ephod and breastplate, where Aaron carries Israel’s names on his shoulders and over his heart, to the robe with its bells, the gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD, and the garments for Aaron’s sons.

sections.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Set Apart, and Holy Garments Are Commanded
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses to take Aaron and his sons to minister to Him as priests and to make holy garments for Aaron “for glory and for beauty” (Exodus 28:2). Skilled artisans whom the LORD has filled with the spirit of wisdom are to make the breastplate, ephod, robe, tunic, turban, and sash.

sections.title: The Ephod and the Names on Aaron’s Shoulders
sections.summary: The ephod is woven of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with two onyx stones set on its shoulder straps, each engraved with six names of the sons of Israel. “So Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders as a memorial” (Exodus 28:12).

sections.title: The Breastplate of Judgment over Aaron’s Heart
sections.summary: The breastplate holds twelve stones in four rows, each engraved with the name of a tribe, and it is fastened to the ephod with gold chains, rings, and a blue cord. Aaron bears the names of the sons of Israel “over his heart” (Exodus 28:29) when he enters the holy place, and with the Urim and Thummim he bears Israel’s judgment before the LORD continually.

sections.title: The Blue Robe with Bells and Pomegranates
sections.summary: The robe of the ephod is all blue, with a reinforced opening for the head and a hem of pomegranates and golden bells. The sound of the bells is heard when Aaron goes into the holy place and comes out, “that he may not die” (Exodus 28:35).

sections.title: The Gold Plate Engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD
sections.summary: A plate of pure gold engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD is fastened to the front of Aaron’s turban. Aaron bears the iniquity of Israel’s holy gifts, “that they may be accepted before the LORD” (Exodus 28:38).

sections.title: Garments for the Priests’ Ministry
sections.summary: Aaron’s tunic, turban, and sash are made, and his sons receive tunics, sashes, and hats for glory and beauty, and all are to be anointed, consecrated, and sanctified as priests. Linen trousers are made for them so that they do not incur iniquity and die when they minister.

1.brief: Moses is to bring Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar to minister to God as priests. God chooses Aaron’s family for the priesthood.
1.explain:
“Now take Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the children of Israel,”

God chooses “Aaron” and “his sons” from among Israel. The priesthood is God’s appointment, not a role anyone may take (Hebrews 5:4).

“that he may minister to Me as priest, Aaron and Aaron’s sons: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.”

They are set apart to minister to God as priests. A priest served before God on behalf of the people. God chooses Aaron’s family for the priesthood.
1.notes: Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10:1–2). Eleazar succeeded Aaron as high priest (Numbers 20:25–28).

2.brief: Holy garments are to be made for Aaron “for glory and for beauty.” The garments honor the priestly office God has given.
2.explain:
“And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty.”

Aaron’s clothes are “holy garments,” set apart for service. They are made “for glory and for beauty.” The garments show the dignity and honor of the priestly office God has given.

3.brief: Moses is to speak to the gifted artisans whom God has filled with the spirit of wisdom, so they can make Aaron’s garments to consecrate him. God supplies the skill needed for holy work.
3.explain:
“So you shall speak to all who are gifted artisans, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom,”

The artisans are “gifted,” literally wise of heart, and God has “filled” them “with the spirit of wisdom.” Their skill is God’s gift.

“that they may make Aaron’s garments, to consecrate him, that he may minister to Me as priest.”

The garments help “consecrate” Aaron for his service. God supplies the skill needed for holy work.
3.notes: Bezalel and Oholiab are later named as the chief craftsmen, filled with the Spirit of God for this work (31:1–6; 35:30–35).

4.brief: The garments are a breastplate, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash, so that Aaron and his sons may minister as priests. The garments set them apart for priestly service.
4.explain:
“And these are the garments which they shall make: a breastplate, an ephod, a robe, a skillfully woven tunic, a turban, and a sash.”

Six garments are listed. Each is described in the verses that follow.

“So they shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons, that he may minister to Me as priest.”

The garments set Aaron and his sons apart for priestly service.

5.brief: The artisans are to use gold, blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and fine linen. The garments use the same rich materials as the sanctuary.
5.explain:
“They shall take the gold, blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and the fine linen,”

The garments use the same costly materials as the tabernacle’s inner curtains and veil (26:1, 31). The high priest is clothed to match the place where he serves.

6.brief: The ephod is made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine woven linen, artistically worked. The ephod is the central outer garment of the high priest.
6.explain:
“and they shall make the ephod of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and fine woven linen, artistically worked.”

“The ephod” is the high priest’s central outer garment, worn over the robe. It was probably like an apron or vest covering the front and back. Gold thread was woven into it (39:3).

7.brief: The ephod has two shoulder straps joined at its edges. The shoulders will carry the memorial stones.
7.explain:
“It shall have two shoulder straps joined at its two edges, and so it shall be joined together.”

Two “shoulder straps” join the front and back. The shoulders will carry the memorial stones.

8.brief: The woven band of the ephod is made of the same materials and workmanship. The band holds the ephod in place.
8.explain:
“And the intricately woven band of the ephod, which is on it, shall be of the same workmanship,”

A woven “band” or belt holds the ephod at the waist.

“made of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and fine woven linen.”

The band uses the same materials and workmanship.

9.brief: Two onyx stones are engraved with the names of the sons of Israel. The tribes’ names will be carried on the high priest.
9.explain:
“Then you shall take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel:”

Two “onyx stones” are engraved with “the names of the sons of Israel,” the twelve tribes.

10.brief: Six names go on each stone, in order of birth. Every tribe is represented.
10.explain:
“six of their names on one stone and six names on the other stone, in order of their birth.”

Six names go on each stone, “in order of their birth.” Every tribe is represented.

11.brief: The stones are engraved like a signet and set in gold. The names are permanently fixed and honored.
11.explain:
“With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, you shall engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel.”

The names are cut “like the engravings of a signet,” carved clearly and permanently, as on a seal.

“You shall set them in settings of gold.”

The stones are mounted in gold. The names are permanently fixed and honored.

12.brief: The stones are placed on the shoulders of the ephod as memorial stones, “So Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders as a memorial.” Aaron carries the whole people before God on his shoulders.
12.explain:
“And you shall put the two stones on the shoulders of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel.”

The stones sit on “the shoulders” as “memorial stones,” a reminder before God.

“So Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders as a memorial.”

The shoulder is the place of strength and burden-bearing. Aaron carries the whole people before God on his shoulders.

13.brief: Settings of gold are made. The settings prepare for fastening the breastplate.
13.explain:
“You shall also make settings of gold,”

Gold “settings” are made for fastening.

14.brief: Two chains of pure gold like braided cords are fastened to the settings. The chains will hold the breastplate in place.
14.explain:
“and you shall make two chains of pure gold like braided cords, and fasten the braided chains to the settings.”

Braided gold “chains” attach to the settings. The chains will hold the breastplate in place (28:22–25).

15.brief: The breastplate of judgment is made with the same workmanship and materials as the ephod. The breastplate carries the people’s judgment before God.
15.explain:
“You shall make the breastplate of judgment.”

“The breastplate of judgment” is a pouch worn on the chest. It is called “of judgment” because it held the Urim and Thummim, through which God gave decisions for Israel (28:30).

“Artistically woven according to the workmanship of the ephod you shall make it: of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and fine woven linen, you shall make it.”

It is made with the same skill and materials as the ephod. The breastplate carries the people’s judgment before God.

16.brief: The breastplate is doubled into a square, a span long and a span wide. The doubled square forms a pouch.
16.explain:
“It shall be doubled into a square: a span shall be its length, and a span shall be its width.”

Folded “into a square,” it measured “a span,” about nine inches, each way. The doubled square forms a pouch.

17.brief: Four rows of stones are set in it, beginning with sardius, topaz, and emerald. Precious stones adorn the breastplate.
17.explain:
“And you shall put settings of stones in it, four rows of stones:”

“Four rows” of precious stones are mounted on the front.

“The first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald; this shall be the first row;”

The first row is named. Precious stones adorn the breastplate.
17.notes: The identification of several of these stones with modern gem names is uncertain.

18.brief: The second row is turquoise, sapphire, and diamond. The stones continue in order.
18.explain:
“the second row shall be a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond;”

The second row continues the list.

19.brief: The third row is jacinth, agate, and amethyst. Each row has its own stones.
19.explain:
“the third row, a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;”

Each row has three stones.

20.brief: The fourth row is beryl, onyx, and jasper, all set in gold. Twelve stones in all are mounted on the breastplate.
20.explain:
“and the fourth row, a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper.”

The fourth row completes the twelve.

“They shall be set in gold settings.”

All are mounted in gold. Twelve stones in all are set on the breastplate.

21.brief: Each stone is engraved with the name of one of the twelve tribes. Every tribe is individually remembered.
21.explain:
“And the stones shall have the names of the sons of Israel, twelve according to their names,”

Each stone bears “the names of the sons of Israel,” one tribe per stone.

“like the engravings of a signet, each one with its own name; they shall be according to the twelve tribes.”

The shoulder stones carry six names each. The breastplate gives every tribe its own stone. Every tribe is individually remembered.

22.brief: Chains of pure gold like braided cords are made for the breastplate. The breastplate is securely attached.
22.explain:
“You shall make chains for the breastplate at the end, like braided cords of pure gold.”

Braided gold “chains” are made for the breastplate. It is securely attached.

23.brief: Two gold rings are put on the two ends of the breastplate. The rings receive the chains.
23.explain:
“And you shall make two rings of gold for the breastplate, and put the two rings on the two ends of the breastplate.”

Two gold rings go on the upper corners. The rings receive the chains.

24.brief: The two gold chains are put in the rings on the ends of the breastplate. The breastplate is linked to the shoulder pieces.
24.explain:
“Then you shall put the two braided chains of gold in the two rings which are on the ends of the breastplate;”

The chains pass through the rings. The breastplate is linked to the shoulder pieces.

25.brief: The other ends of the chains are fastened to the settings on the shoulder straps at the front. These chains secure the breastplate to the front of the shoulder straps.
25.explain:
“and the other two ends of the two braided chains you shall fasten to the two settings, and put them on the shoulder straps of the ephod in the front.”

The other ends of the chains attach to the settings on the shoulder straps. The breastplate hangs from the same shoulders that bear the names.

26.brief: Two more gold rings are put on the inner edge of the breastplate. The lower edge is also secured.
26.explain:
“You shall make two rings of gold, and put them on the two ends of the breastplate, on the edge of it, which is on the inner side of the ephod.”

Two more rings go on the lower inside corners. The lower edge is also secured.

27.brief: Two other gold rings are put on the shoulder straps below, at the seam above the band. The garment is carefully fitted.
27.explain:
“And two other rings of gold you shall make, and put them on the two shoulder straps, underneath the ephod toward its front, right at the seam above the intricately woven band of the ephod.”

Matching rings go on the ephod just above the band. The garment is carefully fitted.

28.brief: The breastplate is tied by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue cord, above the woven band. The cord keeps the breastplate from coming loose from the ephod.
28.explain:
“They shall bind the breastplate by means of its rings to the rings of the ephod, using a blue cord,”

“A blue cord” ties the breastplate’s lower rings to the ephod’s rings.

“so that it is above the intricately woven band of the ephod, and so that the breastplate does not come loose from the ephod.”

The breastplate stays fixed in place. The breastplate cannot come loose from the ephod.

29.brief: “So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the breastplate of judgment over his heart” when he enters the holy place, as a continual memorial before the LORD. Aaron carries the people on his heart as well as his shoulders.
29.explain:
“So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the breastplate of judgment over his heart,”

Aaron carries the names “over his heart.” The heart was the center of affection and thought. He bears the people on his shoulders in strength (28:12) and on his heart in love.

“when he goes into the holy place, as a memorial before the LORD continually.”

Whenever Aaron enters the holy place, the names go with him as “a memorial before the LORD continually.” Aaron carries the people on his heart as well as his shoulders. The shoulders and the heart together picture Jesus, our living High Priest, who has the strength to carry His people and the love to keep them close. He sympathizes with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15–16), and “He always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25).

30.brief: The Urim and Thummim are put in the breastplate over Aaron’s heart, so he bears Israel’s judgment before the LORD continually. The high priest carries the people’s need for God’s decisions into His presence.
30.explain:
“And you shall put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim,”

“The Urim and the Thummim” are placed inside the breastplate. The words likely mean lights and perfections. Scripture does not describe what they were. They were used to seek God’s decision in matters Israel could not settle (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 28:6).

“and they shall be over Aaron’s heart when he goes in before the LORD.”

They rest in the same place as the names.

“So Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel over his heart before the LORD continually.”

He carries the people’s need for God’s decisions into His presence.
30.notes: The Urim and Thummim are mentioned rarely and seem to have fallen out of use after the early monarchy. After the exile, some questions had to wait “till a priest could consult with the Urim and Thummim” (Ezra 2:63).

31.brief: The robe of the ephod is made all of blue. The robe is worn beneath the ephod.
31.explain:
“You shall make the robe of the ephod all of blue.”

“The robe of the ephod” is a long blue garment worn beneath the ephod.

32.brief: The robe has an opening for the head with a woven binding so it will not tear. Its careful finish protects the garment.
32.explain:
“There shall be an opening for his head in the middle of it;”

The robe is pulled on over the head.

“it shall have a woven binding all around its opening, like the opening in a coat of mail, so that it does not tear.”

The neck opening is reinforced “so that it does not tear.” Its careful finish protects the garment.

33.brief: Pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet are made around its hem, with gold bells between them. The pomegranates are decorative shapes worked into the hem, set among the gold bells.
33.explain:
“And upon its hem you shall make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet, all around its hem,”

“Pomegranates” made of colored yarn are attached around the hem.

“and bells of gold between them all around:”

“Bells of gold” hang between the pomegranates. The pomegranates are decorative shapes worked into the hem, set among the gold bells.

34.brief: A gold bell and a pomegranate alternate all around the hem. The pattern runs evenly around the robe.
34.explain:
“a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, upon the hem of the robe all around.”

Bells and pomegranates alternate all the way around. The pattern runs evenly around the robe.

35.brief: Aaron wears it when he ministers, so the sound is heard when he enters and leaves the holy place, “that he may not die.” His service in God’s presence must follow God’s instructions exactly.
35.explain:
“And it shall be upon Aaron when he ministers,”

Aaron wears the robe in his service.

“and its sound will be heard when he goes into the holy place before the LORD and when he comes out, that he may not die.”

The bells sound as he enters and leaves “the holy place.” The text gives the reason only as “that he may not die.” The sound marked his coming and going in God’s presence, and his service had to follow God’s instructions exactly.

36.brief: A plate of pure gold is engraved like a signet, “HOLINESS TO THE LORD.” The high priest bears a public declaration that he belongs to God.
36.explain:
“You shall also make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a signet: HOLINESS TO THE LORD.”

“A plate of pure gold” is engraved “HOLINESS TO THE LORD.” The high priest bears a public declaration that he belongs to God.
36.notes: Zechariah 14:20–21 looks to a day when HOLINESS TO THE LORD will be engraved on the bells of the horses, and every pot in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the LORD of hosts. In the NKJV main text the inscription belongs to the bells; the pots are described as holy without being said to bear the inscription.

37.brief: The plate is tied with a blue cord to the front of the turban. The inscription is placed on his forehead.
37.explain:
“And you shall put it on a blue cord, that it may be on the turban;”

The plate is tied with “a blue cord” to the turban.

“it shall be on the front of the turban.”

It rests “on the front,” across his forehead.

38.brief: The plate is on Aaron’s forehead so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things Israel offers, “that they may be accepted before the LORD.” God provides through Aaron a way for His people to be accepted before Him, with Aaron bearing the iniquity connected to their holy gifts.
38.explain:
“So it shall be on Aaron’s forehead, that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things which the children of Israel hallow in all their holy gifts;”

Aaron wears it so that he “may bear the iniquity of the holy things.” Even Israel’s gifts to God were imperfect. Aaron, set apart as holy to the LORD, bears the guilt connected with them.

“and it shall always be on his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD.”

God provides through Aaron a way for His people and their gifts to be accepted before Him. Christ, the holy High Priest, makes His people’s worship acceptable (Hebrews 7:26–27), and through Him believers offer “spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5).

39.brief: The tunic is woven of fine linen, with a turban of fine linen and a woven sash. The tunic, turban, and sash are the remaining pieces of Aaron’s clothing.
39.explain:
“You shall skillfully weave the tunic of fine linen thread,”

“The tunic” is the long inner garment of fine linen, woven in a pattern.

“you shall make the turban of fine linen, and you shall make the sash of woven work.”

The “turban” and a woven “sash” complete Aaron’s clothing.
39.notes: On the Day of Atonement the high priest set aside the garments of glory and wore plain linen garments to enter the Most Holy Place (Leviticus 16:4, 23–24).

40.brief: Tunics, sashes, and hats are made for Aaron’s sons “for glory and beauty.” The other priests are also clothed with honor.
40.explain:
“For Aaron’s sons you shall make tunics, and you shall make sashes for them.”

Aaron’s sons receive “tunics” and “sashes.”

“And you shall make hats for them, for glory and beauty.”

They also receive “hats.” The other priests are also clothed “for glory and beauty.”

41.brief: Moses is to clothe Aaron and his sons, anoint them, consecrate them, and sanctify them to minister as priests. The garments are part of setting them apart for God.
41.explain:
“So you shall put them on Aaron your brother and on his sons with him.”

Moses is to clothe Aaron and his sons. Chapter 29 describes the ceremony.

“You shall anoint them, consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister to Me as priests.”

They are to be anointed with oil, consecrated, and sanctified. The Hebrew phrase translated “consecrate” reads literally fill their hand, meaning to install them in office. The garments are part of setting them apart for God.

42.brief: Linen trousers are made to cover their nakedness from waist to thighs. Modesty is required in God’s presence.
42.explain:
“And you shall make for them linen trousers to cover their nakedness;”

“Linen trousers” are made as undergarments.

“they shall reach from the waist to the thighs.”

Modesty is required in God’s presence (compare 20:26).

43.brief: Aaron and his sons must wear them when they enter the tabernacle or approach the altar, so they do not incur guilt and die, as a statute forever. Coming near God requires obedience to His instructions.
43.explain:
“They shall be on Aaron and on his sons when they come into the tabernacle of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister in the holy place,”

The priests must wear them whenever they enter the tent or approach the altar.

“that they do not incur iniquity and die.”

Failure to obey brings guilt and death. Coming near God requires obedience to His instructions.

“It shall be a statute forever to him and his descendants after him.”

The rule is permanent for Aaron’s line. Hebrews 7:11–28 explains that a better priesthood has come in Christ, a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
